rules_text:
Rules summary Overview The game plays over a series of turns, until the game end is triggered in one of three ways. If an HQ is captured by a Troop, the capturing player immediately wins. If through region control a player gains a certain number of medals as defined by the map, that player immediately wins. If a player cannot perform any more actions (e.g. they have no tiles to draw and cannot play any tiles), then the game ends. In this case, the player with the most medals wins. In the case of a tie, the player who triggered this end game condition loses. Each player has 24 troops--8 types with 3 of each. During set up, 4 troops are randomly removed from each player's reserve without the players knowing which tiles are removed. The removed tiles are likely different between the two players, creating a mysterious asymmetry. Troops Name Picture Strength Description Notes Kwak X Kwak has no effect, but may be placed on top of any enemy Troop. However, any enemy Troop may also cover it. Skully 1 You may draw 2 Troops from your reserve. If you already have 7 Troops on your rack, you draw only one. Capn 2 You may place 1 extra Troop following normal placement rules and apply its effect. Effects of Troops placed (including Capn) are triggered first, then any special base effects. Jumbo 3 You may choose 1 visible enemy Troop (adjacent to Jumbo) and discard it face up. Troops are adjacent if connected by a single section of path. Hook 4 You may ignore the connection rule and place Hook on any base whether or not it is connected to your H.Q. To place Hook on the enemy HQ (which is not a base), it must be connected to your HQ by your troops. XB-42 5 You may take, at random, 1 Troop from your opponent's rack and discard it face up. Star 6 You may draw 1 Troop from your reserve and place it on your rack. Roxy 7 No effect. Your Turn You can either: Draw 2 Troops from your reserve and place them on your rack. Your rack can hold up to 8 Troops maximum or Play 1 troop from your rack onto a space on the battlefield. You can place it anywhere that fulfills the following conditions: An empty base that is connected to your HQ (this means you must always follow a continuous path from your HQ (starting point) to the troop you are placing, passing only through bases you occupy) A base occupied by any of your troops A base occupied by an enemy troop with a lower strength than your troop Your opponent's HQ. (You cannot place a troop on your own HQ) Each troop has an effect that triggers after placement. If the troop was placed on a special base, you first fully complete the troop's effect before trigger the effect of the special base. If you control a region by occupying all the bases surrounding it, you claim any and all medal(s) currently in that area. If you would draw a 9th troop, you simply do not draw the troop. Battlefields Name Effect of Special Bases Castle Field You may choose 1 of your other troops, no matter where it is, and place it back on your rack. Tropical Pool Only troops with the indicated values can be placed on these special bases and HQ City of Clouds You may draw 1 troop from your reserve and place it on your rack. Volcanic Jungle You may choose 1 enemy troop that is adjacent to this special base. Move it to a base that is adjacent to its starting base, ignoring placement rules. Cursed Cemetery You may choose 1 of your Troops in the discard and place it on your rack. Caribbean Sea No special bases, but is asymmetric with 2 blue HQ and 1 red HQ Station Metal-X Troop effects are not applied on special bases. Battlefield Select 1 of your opponent's Troops at random. It is "frozen" and cannot be placed until the next turn.

[Rating: 1/10] Total and complete luck of the draw fest.  You are at the mercy of what you draw for playing any kind of strategy.

[Rating: 2/10] It's a nifty and clearly well-designed game that doesn’t excite me all that much. I'd be hard-pressed to tell you exactly why, so I'll deflect to my standard criticism of "there will be games where you have no choice but to succumb to the terrible luck of drawing tiles that you absolutely either do not need or cannot use". Lighting fast play time certainly helps quell those woes, though - not much of an investment which makes those cosmic shafts hurt less.

[Rating: 3/10] At a first glance Toy Battle looks like a cute light game: but the more you play it the more you realize how shallow it is. You’re in the hands of the tokens you’re drawing: and more likely than not, usually you don’t have the units you need available.  So the game turns into a luckfest: whoever is lucky enough to have the right units available at the right moment wins.  So much for a game.
